sections.content:
You know *pero* from A1, *sin embargo* from A2 Unit 28, *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1 and *en cambio* from an A2 Unit 28 word list. All of them set one idea against another. This lesson shows five markers that do different jobs, and how they differ from *pero*.

*Pero* joins two clauses inside one sentence, and no comma follows it. The markers below usually start a new clause, after a full stop or a semicolon, and a comma follows them.

• *en cambio*: two things are compared and found different ("whereas", "on the other hand"). It can also sit in the middle of the second clause, between commas.
• *por el contrario*: the opposite of what was just said, or just expected, is true. It often follows a negative.
• *al contrario*: the same idea. It is also the natural one-word answer in conversation.
• *no obstante*: "nevertheless", a more formal *sin embargo*. It admits a fact and goes on in spite of it.
• *ahora bien*: "that said", "now then". It does not say the opposite. It adds a point that limits what you have just accepted.

sections.title: Five markers, five jobs
rows: Mi hermana vive en la ciudad; yo, en cambio, vivo en el campo.
My sister lives in the city; I, on the other hand, live in the country.
No es caro; por el contrario, es muy barato.
It is not expensive; on the contrary, it is very cheap.
—¿Te molesta el ruido? —Al contrario, me gusta.
"Does the noise bother you?" "Quite the opposite, I like it."
Tiene poca experiencia; no obstante, hace un buen trabajo.
He has little experience; nevertheless, he does a good job.
El plan es bueno. Ahora bien, cuesta mucho dinero.
The plan is good. That said, it costs a lot of money.

sections.content: *Pero* is the everyday word: *Es bueno, pero caro.* Use these markers when you want to say what kind of contrast you mean: a comparison (*en cambio*), the opposite (*por el contrario*, *al contrario*), a fact that does not stop you (*no obstante*) or a limit (*ahora bien*).
